caption: IB: @lizzypalios How many times have I thought, "Can anybody read the room here?!!" I could be knee-deep in an obviously unavailable moment and it's "Mom, can I get a snack?" "Mom! I need you!" followed by a thousand rapid-fire questions. Or I'm merging into traffic in a torrential downpour and suddenly everyone in the car needs me. 😮‍💨 But what feels "obvious" to me may not actually be obvious to my child. There's no formal milestone for "reading the room." It takes a mix of skills, like noticing what's happening around you, understanding someone else may be having a different experience, deciding how important your need is, and sometimes waiting. Those skills develop differently in different kids. Your child may know you're stressed and still desperately need to tell you their sock feels weird. To them, that sock is VERY important. Some kids easily notice facial expressions and tone. Some notice but have a hard time waiting once they have a thought. Some do much better when people communicate clearly and directly, and others are highly sensitive to any tension around them. Neurodivergent kids can fall anywhere along this range, and missing an unspoken cue does not mean a child lacks empathy. So rather than expecting kids to just "read the room," we can make the room easier to read. Instead of, "Can't you see I'm busy?"Try: "I'm merging into traffic and need to concentrate. Unless someone is hurt or unsafe, hold that thought." We can explain context so kids don't have to guess:"Dad's on the phone. Let's wait until he's finished." And we can teach what needs our attention right away.Someone is hurt or unsafe? Tell me now.You want me to open your granola bar? That can wait. Over time, we're helping kids understand context and know that when something isn't clear, direct communication works too. With practice, many kids will need less explanation. Some will always do better when people are clear, and that's a pretty great communication skill for the rest of us too. Anyone else's kid have an incredible ability to need you at the exact moment you are least available? 😂

caption: Stitch with: @lyssa.hamblin on IG  Your kid just pointed at someone in the grocery store and asked about them. Loudly. 😬 What you do in the next few seconds teaches more than you’d think. That cringe moment is so normal. A lot of us grew up being hushed and hurried along. But kids read our faces faster than our words. When we freeze or shush, they learn the difference is something scary or off-limits. And they don’t stop noticing, but they do stop asking us about it. A few things that help, from the exam room and from real life: ✔️ Keep it short and honest. Little kids need one true sentence, not a lecture. “His legs work differently, so the wheelchair helps him get around.” Done. ✔️ Find the common ground. Point out what your child shares with that person. “She loves the swings too!” That turns a stranger into a possible friend. ✔️ Be careful with “we’re all the same” messages. The intent is kind, but kids raised on colorblind messages actually have a harder time spotting unfairness. ✔️ Real time together beats any script. Preschoolers who spend time with peers who have disabilities tend to be more accepting. Inclusive classrooms, playdates, books, and shows all count. ✔️ They copy what we do. Who we sit next to, how we talk about the new kid in class, whether we wave first. And if you fumble it in the moment? That’s okay. Circle back later: “Remember the boy at the park? I’ve been thinking about your question.”  Kids learn kindness the way they learn to walk, lots of practice with us close by. That’s why we made Happy’s Big Mistake. 💛 Watch the full Happy, Pappy? episode, “Happy’s Big Mistake,” on the Happy, Pappy YouTube channel.  Share this with a parent who’s had the grocery store moment. caption: It’s dinnertime, everyone’s exhausted, and your kid’s still using the iPad after you’ve asked them to put it away. You ask them again, and wait — am I talking to a wall or my child? Why do they never listen the first time?!  OK, hear us out – how many times have you said something like this:  “If you don’t put your shoes on, we’re not going to school.” <kid refuses shoes, still goes to school>  "If you don’t stop screaming, we are going to land this airplane. No more Disneyland if you don’t stop screaming.” <airplane doesn’t land mid flight, we still go to Disneyland>  “Stop splashing the water or we’re getting out of the tub. I said stop splashing or we’re getting out of the tub. I mean it this time! Stop splashing!”  What’s the common denominator here? We’re not *meaning* what we say.  Sure, it might seem obvious to us that we’re not ACTUALLY going to land the plane, but toddler brains are still developing.🧠  They’re still figuring out cause & effect & how the world works. These types of “threats” hold weight to them.  “Dad says no more iPad? Well, he also said he was going to land the plane last week, and that didn’t happen. So does he really mean it this time?”  And in scenarios like the bath splashing, if we beg, plead, & negotiate rather than swoop in with the boundary, a thought pattern starts to develop: “Hey, if I just ignore mom/dad, I’m going to get 10 more mins splashing!”  So, how do we get them to listen the first time? ✨MEAN WHAT WE SAY.✨ How? Hold firm, calm, consistent, confident, swift boundaries the first time, every time. 💯  This sounds like:  “When you splash in the tub, it tells me you’re all done. It looks like you're having a hard time. I'm taking you out. It's ok to be sad about that."  “Time to leave the park. I know it’s hard to leave the park, I'm going to hold your hand/pick you up to help you leave now."  When we follow through with the boundary quickly, every time, our toddlers will learn that we mean what we say, so we’ll see MORE listening & LESS tantrums over time.🎉. #biglittlefeelings #resilientkids #toddlerlife #tantrums #parenting101

caption: There’s no denying it: seeing your toddler hit can be REALLY scary/triggering as a parent. 🆘 It’s natural to panic, yell, “NO stop! NO!” + want to give out a big bad punishment for a big bad behavior. But, hear us out. Your toddler is constantly craving your attention. So, when you give a big reaction to hitting, they’re not going to remember the punishment or the anger. They’re going to remember, “Ooh hitting made mommy pay attention to me! Let’s do that again!” 😑 The more attention you give to a behavior, that’s the behavior you’ll see more of. So, if you have a big, huge reaction to hitting? Guess what you’ll see more of: Hitting. Toddler’s brains aren’t fully developed yet, so they don’t have the mental ability to think, “I’m feeling mad. I’m going to take a deep breath and then tell them what I want/need.” The good news? We can teach impulse control & better behavior. We can teach our child that their FEELING (anger) is ok. And their BEHAVIOR (hitting) is not. Here’s your go-to game plan: 1️⃣ Stay calm in the moment. Let your calm be contagious when your child is in a heightened moment. 2️⃣ OK the Feeling. “You’re feeling angry/sad/silly right now. It’s OK to feel angry/silly/sad.” 3️⃣Hold the Boundary. “It’s not OK to hit. I’m going to move your sister over here to keep everyone safe.” 4️⃣ Teach Coping Skills after the moment has passed. Teach coping skills during a calm, unrelated moment—when the 🧠 learns best. Lastly, remember how toddlers want our attention more than ANYTHING? We can leverage that by doing what we call “Spotlight the Right.” So when your toddler is playing gently, or they use coping skills instead of hitting, make a BIG deal to see more of that behavior. “Yes! You’re playing so gently with your sister!” “Yay! You took some deep tiger breaths instead of hitting!” ✨Struggling with aggressive behavior? Want to teach coping skills + learn to discipline in a way that WORKS? Our course, Winning the Toddler Stage, is here to help! For parents/caregivers with kids ages 1-6.
